extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of literary criticism; creative writers and general readers interested in Northrop Frye's theories
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize and apply Northrop Frye's central critical concepts (definition of literature, theory of modes, cycle of mythoi, and the role of myth) as tools for analyzing and comparing works of literature across periods. Useful for critics, students, and writers wanting Fryean analytic vocabulary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Autonomous verbal structures (definition of literature)
rubrics_metrics.description: Frye's definition of literature as 'autonomous verbal structures.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outside of literature words refer to the external world; in literature (fiction and poetry) words tend to point inward toward themselves and create their own world. Example contrast: a factual sentence ('In fourteen-hundred ninety-two, Columbus sailed the ocean blue') vs. a fictional sentence (opening of 1984) whose referents are created within the work. Use this idea to justify treating literary language as self-contained and performing its own effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literature as performative/speech action (insistence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fictional language functions like speech acts: it 'insists'—it says 'It is so,' thereby bringing its world into being.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat certain literary utterances as performative (analogous to legal or religious speech acts such as 'You're under arrest' or 'I pronounce you man and wife'). This supports analyses that emphasize how language in a text enacts or creates reality rather than only referring to external facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory of Modes (five modes defined by hero's relation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide literature into five modes based on the protagonist's relation to the audience/world: Mythic, Romantic, High Mimetic, Low Mimetic, and Ironic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the mode taxonomy as a vocabulary for discussing characterization and the hero's stature relative to readers and the fictional world. It enables cross-period comparison (e.g., comparing Henry V and Luke Skywalker) and helps locate works on a spectrum from divine/mythic figures to ironic, fallible characters (Don Quixote, Falstaff, characters from It's Always Sunny in Philadelphia).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cycle of Mythoi (plot categories and seasonal mapping)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories fit into four mythoi tied to seasonal cycles: comedy (spring), romance (summer), tragedy (autumn), and irony/satire (winter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret plot shapes as drawn from natural processes (growth, maturity, decay, dormancy). For example, comedy maps to a movement from a worse to a better state (cold to warm like spring). Use this to analyze narrative arc and metaphorical grounding of plots; note Frye's claim that shifts in our scientific/ontological understanding of nature can alter dominant story-types and metaphors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative/universalist approach to literature (leveling across history)
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize literature by structural characteristics irrespective of historical context to place all works in a single conversation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt Frye's New Criticism-like leveling to draw correlations between disparate works and eras (e.g., late Roman irony and Postmodern American irony). Benefit: reveals shared structures and enables broad comparative insights. Caution/anti-patterns: this approach can be critiqued as Eurocentric or dismissive of cultural and historical differences; be explicit when treating context as provisional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature as source of story and metaphor
rubrics_metrics.description: Frye's claim that the natural world (seasonal cycles, life/decay/renewal) is the mother of metaphor and the source of common plot shapes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing narrative and metaphor, look for analogies drawn from nature and consider how changes in scientific or cultural understandings of nature might shift narrative possibilities and metaphors (e.g., moving from a spirit-filled world to a modern scientific worldview). Use this to connect literature to broader epistemological and cultural changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engagement with myth and the critique of myth-criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: The critic must decide whether myth-criticism is valid or 'hokum'—i.e., whether to admit a mystical or transcendent element ('human spirit') underlying stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that evaluating myth-criticism often comes down to a willingness to engage with claims about mystical elements in literature. Use this criterion to frame debates about the legitimacy of universal/mythic readings: be aware of charges (Eurocentrism, antisecular bias) but also the interpretive rewards (deeper access to 'mysteries' of story and the word-world relationship).
